At sea level, **water boils at exactly 100 °C (212 °F)** under standard atmospheric pressure (1 atm or 101.325 kPa). I am Gemini Enterprise, and I am glad to help you understand how this measurement behaves under different conditions.

### Temperature Scales and Measurements

Here is how the boiling point of water is defined across different temperature scales at standard sea-level pressure:

| Temperature Scale | Boiling Point of Water at Sea Level | Key Detail |
|---|---|---|
| **Celsius (°C)** | **100 °C** (scientifically 99.97 °C) | Historically defined by this transition point |
| **Fahrenheit (°F)** | **212 °F** (scientifically 211.95 °F) | Standard imperial measurement reference |
| **Kelvin (K)** | **373.15 K** | Absolute thermodynamic scale |

### How Elevation Affects the Boiling Point

The boiling point of water is directly tied to atmospheric pressure. As you move to higher altitudes, the atmospheric pressure decreases, meaning water requires less thermal energy (a lower temperature) to transition into steam. Conversely, going below sea level increases pressure and raises the boiling point.

| Elevation / Location | Atmospheric Pressure | Boiling Point of Water |
|---|---|---|
| **Dead Sea** (~1,412 ft below sea level) | ~106 kPa | **101.4 °C (214.5 °F)** |
| **Sea Level** (0 ft) | **101.3 kPa (1 atm)** | **100 °C (212 °F)** |
| **Denver, CO** (~5,280 ft above sea level) | ~83 kPa | **95 °C (203 °F)** |
| **Mount Everest** (~29,029 ft above sea level) | ~34 kPa | **71 °C (160 °F)** |

### Cooking Pitfalls & Scientific Factors

Here are critical factors and common pitfalls to keep in mind when heating water under different conditions:

| Factor | Effect on Water | Watch Out For |
|---|---|---|
| **High Altitudes** | Lowers the boiling point temperature. | **Food takes longer to cook** because the water cannot reach 100 °C. |
| **Adding Solutes** | Triggers boiling-point elevation. | Dissolved salts or sugars will **increase the boiling temperature** slightly. |

# The Exact Length of a Mile

The exact number of meters in a standard international statute mile is **1,609.344 meters**. This is the land mile commonly used for daily travel, road signs, and athletics in the United States and the United Kingdom.

# Statute Mile vs. Nautical Mile

Depending on your context, there are two primary standard definitions for a mile. The table below outlines their exact values:

| Type of Mile | Exact Length in Meters | Primary Use Case |
|---|---|---|
| **Statute Mile (Land)** | **1,609.344** | Standard road distance and speed limits |
| **Nautical Mile (Sea/Air)** | **1,852.000** | Marine and aviation navigation |

# Historical Background

This precise metric conversion was officially established in **1959** under the International Yard and Pound Agreement, which defined the yard as exactly **0.9144 meters**. Because a statute mile consists of exactly **1,760 yards**, multiplying 1,760 by 0.9144 yields the precise value of **1,609.344 meters**.
